transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO, Lagoon Robotics), Ethan Cho (Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Head of Infra)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on model selection for Lagoon Robotics' conversational and multimodal fleet assistant. Main topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, open model comparisons (Llama/Mistral/Falcon), context length needs (32k vs 64k), multilingual support, and function/tool-calling for robotics control hooks. Agreed next steps: share pricing, run a short benchmark on Redwood Hosted with a 32k context test and multilingual prompt set, schedule SE deep dive for infra and security (VPC/KMS).

Topics: model family tradeoffs, context windows, latency/cost, tool-calling/function calling, private deployment constraints (air-gapped robots), SOC2/KMS requirements, rollout plan and success criteria.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we got about 55 minutes. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Carlos from our SE team.
[00:00:08] Priya Nair: Hi Maya, hi Carlos. Thanks for carving out time. We wanted to focus specifically on model selection — we already have some initial experiments on open models and trying to figure out hosted vs dedicated vs private for our fleet.
[00:00:20] Carlos Ortega: Great, yeah that's exactly what we do with customers at this stage. Can you give us a quick overview of your main workloads and any hard constraints?
[00:00:28] Ethan Cho: Sure. We run a conversational agent on board our inspection robots — it's a mix of short dialog and longer reasoning chains when debugging. Typical convo lengths range from a few turns (200–500 tokens) up to 8–10k tokens when the agent walks through multi-step diagnostic traces. For some use cases we need up to ~30k tokens context because we attach logs and recent sensor data. Multilingual is important — English, Japanese, and Spanish primarily. Latency target is sub-300ms for short queries, and we can tolerate higher for long reasoning.
[00:00:57] Liam O'Connor: Also important: some customers require that inference happens in a private network or even air-gapped environments. So we're evaluating whether Redwood Private (on-prem/VPC) is necessary or if Dedicated with strict VPC peering is enough.
[00:01:10] Maya Chen: Good context — thanks. A couple quick clarifying Qs: when you say 30k context, is that peak for single request including attachments?
[00:01:16] Ethan Cho: Yeah that's peak. Most common is under 8k though.
[00:01:20] Carlos Ortega: Ok. For model families we typically think about a couple axes: 1) context window support (32k, 64k), 2) latency vs quality tradeoffs, 3) multilingual performance, and 4) tool-calling/function calling support. For open models we see Llama 2 variants, Mistral, Falcon, and newer mixtures like Mixtral. There are also smaller optimized models for latency.
[00:01:40] Priya Nair: We've run some internal tests with Llama 2 70B and a couple of Mistral checkpoints. Llama scaled well but token cost and latency were higher; Mistral seemed faster but had some hallucination on longer traces.
[00:01:53] Carlos Ortega: That's consistent with other customers. For 30k context, we recommend either models with explicit 32k/64k variants or using our KV cache + prefix caching to stitch in logs. Redwood supports automatic K V cache handling but if you need true 64k native model you may want a model that was trained for that window — some community models have 32k patches.
[00:02:12] Ethan Cho: How do you handle tool-calling? We need the model to emit structured calls that our orchestration layer consumes to trigger robot actions — so deterministic function calling, safety checks, and ability to fall back to a plan-only response.
[00:02:24] Carlos Ortega: We support structured function/tool calling and can enforce schemas. There are two approaches: 1) use the model's function-calling primitives (hosted) and have Redwood translate to your functions, or 2) send the model a separate tool sandbox/eval so it reasons about a plan and then we validate before execute. We can also add a policy layer that rejects any call outside allowed operations.
[00:02:44] Priya Nair: Any limitations with open models on function calling? We had trouble with some forks not respecting function schema strictly.
[00:02:51] Maya Chen: Right — fidelity varies. We usually recommend testing the exact checkpoints you plan to deploy. For Hosted we have a model catalog with curated open models and performance profiles. For Dedicated/Private you can pin a variant or use a Redwood-verified build. Carlos, maybe expand on pinned variants and rollouts?
[00:03:06] Carlos Ortega: Sure. With Dedicated or Private you can pin a specific model build and we provide canary rollouts and A/B routing so you can test new variants on a percentage of traffic. That helps with hallucination/regression control. Also, our Optimize toolkit can suggest quantization profiles for cost/perf tradeoffs.
[00:03:20] Liam O'Connor: On security — SOC2 is a must. We also need KMS integration, audit logs, and SSO. If we go Private, we need HSM support for key material and offline deployment options.
[00:03:30] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2, and we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. For Private we can integrate with HSMs and support air-gapped installs — that's something our Solutions Eng team has done for regulated robotics customers. I'll add the SOC2 deck and our security pack in the follow-ups.
[00:03:44] Ethan Cho: Cost — very important. For hosted/paying per token, we need clear numbers for long-context sessions. Are there batching or caching tools that reduce per-token bill?
[00:03:54] Carlos Ortega: Yes. Redwood's caching and batching reduce token counts by deduplicating prefixes and storing KV cache so repeated context doesn't get re-sent. For long-horizon traces you can also use retrieval augmentation where only embeddings are sent and the model sees condensed context. We can run a cost estimate once we see sample prompts.
[00:04:10] Priya Nair: For multilingual, did you say specific models are better? We need high quality in Japanese especially technical language.
[00:04:17] Carlos Ortega: Mistral variants and some Falcon forks have decent multilingual coverage; Llama2 multilingual behavior depends on the fine-tuning. For highest fidelity in Japanese technical docs, we recommend testing with native prompts. We can run a 1k prompt set in Japanese and measure BLEU/ROUGE-ish heuristics plus subjective evals.
[00:04:33] Maya Chen: Quick note on latency: if sub-300ms is a strict SLO for short queries, Dedicated or Hosted on GPU-optimized pools with smaller models or quantized variants works well. Private on-prem may need careful hardware selection to meet that.
[00:04:47] Liam O'Connor: What about quantization and model size? We currently have a handful of on-prem GPUs (A100 class) but also want cost savings.
[00:04:55] Carlos Ortega: Quantization helps a lot — int8/int4 can reduce footprint and improve throughput. Redwood's runtime picks kernels and quantization-friendly paths. There's a tradeoff with output quality; we use evals to ensure acceptance criteria are met.
[00:05:07] Ethan Cho: Any recommendations for a starting model for our use case? 32k vs 64k?
[00:05:11] Carlos Ortega: Given your peak 30k, I'd recommend starting with 32k-native variants if possible and use KV cache for attachments; or pick a 64k-capable community model if you want native full-window. Practically, a Llama2- or Mistral-based 32k checkpoint quantized to int8 might give the best latency/cost balance for short queries while handling longer traces with caching.
[00:05:29] Priya Nair: We also have strict data residency for a subset of customers in Japan and EU. How does Redwood support region pinning?
[00:05:36] Maya Chen: We offer region pinning on Hosted (subject to available regions) and Dedicated/Private obviously give full control. For compliance we can also provide contract language and data residency statements.
[00:05:45] Liam O'Connor: On private deployments, is the control plane still Redwood-managed? We need a private control plane or self-hosted control plane.
[00:05:52] Carlos Ortega: For Private deployments we can offer a customer-managed control plane option; it depends on the package. We can also do a hybrid where the inference plane is on-prem and the control plane is in a VPC with mutual TLS.
[00:06:03] Priya Nair: Sounds good. For the benchmark pilot — what's realistic to expect?
[00:06:09] Carlos Ortega: We can spin up a Hosted trial, run a 32k context benchmark with your prompts, measure latency, token cost, and function-calling fidelity. That usually takes 1–2 weeks to set up and run if you can provide prompts and sample logs. For Dedicated pilots we can provision a small reserved pool but that adds provisioning lead time.
[00:06:27] Maya Chen: So next steps recap: Maya will send pricing and security docs; Carlos will schedule the SE deep dive/benchmark; Priya will provide sample prompt sets and multilingual examples. Any other stakeholders we should loop in?
[00:06:38] Priya Nair: I'll pull in our compliance lead and a robotics safety engineer for the follow-up technical deep dive.
[00:06:44] Ethan Cho: Also, can you add notes about tool-calling safety patterns you mentioned? The sandbox + policy layer sounds promising.
[00:06:50] Carlos Ortega: Absolutely. I'll include a short doc and an example schema for safe function calls.
[00:06:56] Maya Chen: Cool. Anything else on the model selection front?
[00:07:00] Priya Nair: One last thing — can Redwood host a model that we've fine-tuned in-house? We might have a fine-tuned Llama fork with RLHF on troubleshooting dialogs.
[00:07:07] Carlos Ortega: Yes, you can bring-your-own-model for Dedicated or Private. For Hosted we may be able to host it as a customer-owned model under certain terms; we can discuss access controls and pinning. We'll need to vet the binary for licensing compatibility.
[00:07:20] Ethan Cho: Licensing is a concern — some models have restrictions. We'll list which checkpoints we plan to use.
[00:07:25] Maya Chen: Great. I'll follow up with the SOC2 report, security pack, and pricing. Carlos will run the benchmark scope doc.
[00:07:33] Priya Nair: Thanks, that's useful. We'll be in touch.
[00:07:36] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[00:07:38] (meeting wraps; remainder of the time used for scheduling next call)
